Eggs of the Western spadefoot (Spea hammondii) typically hatch after a developmental period of approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days] when incubated at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a duration that aligns with the relatively fast embryonic development observed in arid-adapted anurans. Upon eclosion, the newly emerged larvae possess a modest wet weight at birth of only 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly 1.7 millimeters that characterizes this species. This minimal initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. During the subsequent free-swimming tadpole stage, individuals undergo a period of rapid growth and development. The time from hatching until the completion of metamorphosis, measured at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], has been recorded as approximately 75 days , though the literature notes considerable variation ranging from 30 to 80 days depending on local thermal regimes and resource availability. This metamorphic transition marks a critical allometric shift in the species' life cycle.

Females of Spea hammondii attain an ultimate wet weight of 10.88 grams [Wwi = 10.88 grams], a body size that positions them as moderately large among North American spadefoots. This asymptotic mass, which reflects the maximum recorded body mass for adult females, is achieved following a period of sustained juvenile growth. The onset of sexual maturation, or puberty, is not reached immediately upon completing metamorphosis. Instead, data indicate that the time since metamorphosis at puberty for females reaches approximately 547.5 days [tp = approximately 547.5 days] when animals are maintained under controlled thermal conditions, specifically at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This extended period of post-metamorphic development likely reflects the time required for individuals to accumulate sufficient energy reserves and attain the necessary somatic size to support gonadal maturation and the associated energetic costs of reproduction. The reproductive system is thus activated only after a substantial delay relative to the larval-juvenile transition.

Reproductive output in the Western spadefoot is strongly tied to the brief, ephemeral pools that characterize its arid habitat. Females, when reproductively active, typically deposit a single clutch of eggs per year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs per year] at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] during the brief window following heavy seasonal rains. This low frequency of reproductive events is a common strategy among explosive-breeding desert anurans. Within that single annual event, a female can produce approximately 500 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 500 eggs per clutch] over the course of the breeding season when measured at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This clutch size, which represents the maximum reproductive output possible under favorable environmental conditions, yields a daily reproduction rate of approximately 1.37 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1.37 eggs per day]. The constraint of a single annual spawning event is likely a direct consequence of the unpredictable nature of the desert rainfall that triggers breeding, limiting opportunities for multiple clutches within a single active season.

Longevity records for Spea hammondii, extrapolated from data on the closely related congener Scaphiopus couchii, suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 2,555 days [am = approximately 2,555 days] under natural conditions at a mean ambient temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This equates to roughly seven years, a relatively extended lifespan for a small-bodied desert anuran and one that likely facilitates multiple reproductive events across an individual's lifetime. The basal metabolic rate, measured as the standard oxygen consumption of resting adults, was recorded at 0.0125 milliliters per hour [JOi = 0.0125 milliliters per hour] when the animals were held at the same thermal reference point of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This modest metabolic demand is typical of fossorial and arid-adapted amphibians, which frequently exhibit reduced resting metabolic rates as an energy-conserving strategy during the prolonged dry seasons spent in underground aestivation, thereby buffering them against the energetic challenges of an unpredictable environment.

The life history of Spea hammondii is a classic example of adaptation to ephemeral and unpredictable aquatic habitats. The initial wet mass of a neonate, at only 0.0026 grams [Wwb = only 0.0026 grams], highlights the extreme energy limitation at the very start of life. Pond-drying risk exerts a strong selective pressure, favoring rapid larval development; the 75-day interval from hatching to metamorphosis (75 days)  at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] represents a balance between the need for quick emergence and the physiological costs of accelerated growth. The ultimate adult size for females, at 10.88 grams [Wwi = 10.88 grams], is a direct outcome of the trade-off between reaching a size sufficient for high fecundity and the constraints of a short growing season. The species' remarkable longevity of 2,555 days [am = 2,555 days] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] provides a demographic buffer, allowing individuals to skip reproduction in drought years while still maintaining a lifetime positive reproductive output through a single annual clutch event.
